WATER GUIDE

Saltwater flats

Learn to spot tails, shadows, and moving fish on shallow flats. Lead the fish with a light lure or fly and stay ready for the first run.

KEY FACTS

Orvis teaches flats fishing through fish spotting, tides, guide communication, fly selection and presentation.

Orvis Learning Center — Saltwater inshore flats ↗

Bonefish and other flats fish can be approached on foot, with small movements of a fly near the bottom.

Orvis — Wading the Flats ↗

Bonefish on fly require a line-hand strip set rather than an upward trout-style rod lift.

Orvis — How to Hook More Bonefish by Sight-Setting ↗

Rising water can bring fish onto flats, while falling water directs them toward deeper areas.

Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission — Saltwater Fishing Tips ↗

Look for movement before color

Slow down before you cast. Scan a short patch of water through polarized glasses, then shift your gaze farther out. A moving shadow, a tail tip, or a small push of water can reveal a fish before its outline becomes clear. Sand patches make good places to learn. On grass or broken bottom, follow the direction of travel rather than staring at one dark shape.

Keep the sun behind or beside you when the route allows. From a skiff, agree on distance and clock-face directions with the person on the platform. From shore, take small steps and stop often. Stay far enough away that your line and shadow miss the fish. When you find one, decide where the lure should land before you lift the rod. An unhurried first cast is often the best chance.

Lead the fish and let the fly settle

For bonefish, start with a small shrimp-style fly or jig suited to the depth. Use less weight in very shallow water and more when the fly must sink before the fish arrives. Cast ahead of the fish, not onto it. Let the presentation settle, then use a short pull to draw attention. If the fish turns toward it, watch closely and avoid dragging the bait into its face.

Keep the fly rod low. When the fish takes and the line tightens, set with a firm pull of the line hand. Clear loose line from feet and fittings as the fish runs. With spinning gear, a small shrimp lure offers a similar quiet presentation. Match the outfit to the target: a bonefish setup is no substitute for tackle intended for large tarpon or giant trevally.

Follow the tide without losing your exit

A rising tide can let fish spread onto shallow feeding areas. As the water falls, check channels and the edges that lead toward deeper water. Spend time watching how fish enter and leave your flat. A local tide chart gives you a starting time, while the water at your feet tells you what is happening now.

Choose calm, bright conditions when you want to learn fish spotting. A low sun, cloud, or wind ripple makes the job harder, even when fish are present. In poor visibility, work a known edge with controlled casts instead of chasing uncertain shapes. Before you wade out, identify a route that stays usable as the tide rises. Avoid crossing deep channels to reach a distant tail. Leave room in the day to return against wind or current.

Keep the deck clear and the flat quiet

Lay out only the line you can manage. Strip it into a clean part of the deck or a suitable line basket, away from buckles and loose bags. Check the leader knot and hook point before each new fish. A short practice cast shows whether the fly turns over in the wind. Wear glasses and keep hooks away from the guide and your partner.

Wade only on suitable ground with local knowledge of holes, rays, and sharp bottom. Wear footwear matched to the surface. Avoid living coral and fragile grass. Give another angler or skiff a wide berth, and never run through a flat someone is stalking. Bring the fish to hand promptly, support it in the water, and release it without a long photo session. Carry drinking water and cover exposed skin.

SHOPPING LIST

Saltwater flats shopping list

  • Flats boots

    Hard soles for coral, shells and sand.

    Check price ↗

  • Polarized sunglasses (amber or copper lens)

    Essential to spot fish on the flat.

    Check price ↗

  • Sun hoodie

    UPF shirt with a hood for all-day sun.

    Check price ↗

  • Buff face cover

    Protects your face and neck.

    Check price ↗

  • Saltwater fly or spinning combo

    Ask the guide what weight they use.

    Check price ↗

  • Reef-safe sunscreen

    Many flats destinations require it.

FIVE DECISIONS TO MAKE
  1. Clean the glasses.
  2. Clear loose line from the deck.
  3. Lead the fish with the cast.
  4. Match fly weight to depth.
  5. Check the wading exit.
